title: When the Visitor Burns
premise: Hazel Ravensworth, a pest controller who moved to the village of Marrow Fen to disappear, is called to investigate scratching in the church walls and finds handprints burned into the plaster—prints that match his own. The bell that rings at night was melted down in 1911, and its sound peels back the village's shared forgetting: in 1974, the townsfolk drowned a child they believed a witch, and every adult took something from her—her name, her shoes, her voice—to seal their silence. Hazel's own fingerprints are there because his father was one of them, and Hazel has carried her stolen name inside him all along. To end the haunting before the harvest moon completes its rise, he must return what was taken, confessing his family's part to a village that would rather burn him than remember.
about_author: H. M. Pemberton is the pen name of a former rural surveyor who spent a decade documenting abandoned churches across East Anglia. They write horror about small communities and the debts that outlive the people who incurred them.

chapters.title: The Scratching in the Wall
chapters.summary: POV Hazel. Called to St. Aldhelm's at dusk, Hazel finds no rats—only five-fingered prints seared into the plaster behind the vestry, still warm. He tells himself it's a prank, but takes a rubbing anyway. Emotional beat: the practiced calm of a man whose explanations are starting to cost more than the truth.

chapters.title: A Bell That Isn't There
chapters.summary: POV Hazel. At 3 a.m. the church bell rings; the parish records confirm it was melted down in 1911. Villagers claim not to hear it, though doors lock and lights die street by street as it tolls. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening—the village hears nothing because the bell is ringing for him alone.

chapters.title: What Mrs. Okafor Kept
chapters.summary: POV Hazel. Elderly Edith Okafor, the last resident born before 1950, recognizes the rubbing and goes white. She gives him a shoebox of newspaper clippings about a missing child in 1974, then begs him to leave town by Friday. Emotional beat: dread arriving through another person's terror.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Quiet
chapters.summary: POV Hazel, with flashbacks. Why Hazel came to Marrow Fen: after his father's death he found a child's shoe among his belongings and burned it rather than ask questions. Now the scratches appear on his own bedroom wall. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing—the past he fled has been living in his luggage.

chapters.title: The Harvest Committee
chapters.summary: POV Hazel. The village council, led by genial squire Tom Verrity, offers Hazel money and a new contract if he stops investigating. Their warmth is flawless and rehearsed, like men reciting lines learned long ago. Emotional beat: power's polite menace—belonging offered as a bribe for silence.

chapters.title: Under the Floor of the Vestry
chapters.summary: POV Hazel. Following the heat in the walls, Hazel pries up the vestry floor and finds a cache: a name tag reading 'WREN', a pair of small shoes, and a tape recorder labeled 1974. The tape holds a child's voice singing the harvest hymn. Emotional beat: grief and revulsion—the taken things are real, catalogued like trophies.

chapters.title: Everyone Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: POV alternating Hazel/Edith. Edith confesses: the village drowned Wren Halloway believing she cursed the crops, and each participant kept one thing of hers so none could fully remember or forget. Hazel realizes his father kept her name—and gave it, twisted, to his own child. Emotional beat: the floor dropping out of identity itself.

chapters.title: They Come for the Box
chapters.summary: POV Hazel. Verrity and half the village surround Hazel's cottage at moonrise-minus-three, demanding the relics 'for the good of everyone.' When he refuses, the burned handprints bloom across his windows like frost. Emotional beat: siege horror—the community's belonging revealed as a closed fist.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: POV Hazel. On the harvest moon's final climb, Hazel carries Wren's things into the flooded quarry where she died, speaking her true name aloud—his own middle name, surrendered. The villagers follow, weeping as memory floods back. The water rises to meet the moon. Emotional beat: sacrificial climax—giving back the self he built on theft.

chapters.title: After the Ringing Stops
chapters.summary: POV Hazel, weeks later. The bell is silent; the prints have cooled to ordinary stains. The village remembers everything now, and some cannot look at Hazel—but Edith plants marigolds on Wren's unmarked grave, and Hazel stays, finally visible and finally home. Emotional beat: bruised resolution—belonging earned through truth, not silence.
